body_markdown:
When hot-rodder and[YouTuber David Freiburger](https://www.youtube.com/@TheDavidFreiburger) needed a new engine for his 1970 Plymouth Duster—the “Crop Duster” used on several episodes of[Roadkill](https://www.hagerty.com/media/people/exclusive-whats-next-for-david-freiburger-after-roadkill/) —he found what looked like a solid deal on a freshly rebuilt 383 Mopar big-block. Because it had never been fired up, it was anyone’s guess if it had been assembled properly. With so many unknowns, there was lots to scrutinize. It was a good thing he did, as the engine inspection prevented some major headaches.


David’s routing checks are a good road map to making sure any rebuilt engine will run as desired. Although he started with what was touted as a buttoned-up engine, the only way to check critical dimensions was to disassemble it, at least partially. The more parts came off the engine, the more was revealed.


The .060”-over pistons are flat tops, and they’re .026” from the top of the deck. That’s not great for the compression ratio, and not great for quench (the clearance from piston to head), either. With the .039″ compressed thickness of the head gasket and 80cc combustion chambers, the result is a 9.45:1 compression ratio. That makes for an engine that will run fine on pump gas, but it’s also leaving a lot on the table.


David checked inside the engine and found good main journal and rod journal clearance, but it was lacking assembly lube, and the oil pan pickup was nearly an inch from the bottom of the sump. This engine would have been in trouble had he fired it up without addressing those problems.


There were a few more issues, like an incorrect timing pointer, and the fact that the hydraulic flat tappet cam included with the engine would have dangerously little piston-to-valve clearance. The solution was a new hydraulic flat tappet cam with 216/228 degrees of duration at .050” valve lift, .454/.480 inches of total lift, and 112 degrees of lobe separation.


Even with its issues, there was plenty to love about the engine. It had a set of 440 Source “Stealth” aluminum heads, for one. They offer the same profile and casting plug on the end of the heads as the factory iron castings while flowing a lot more air. 440 Source claims as-cast flow of 290 CFM through the 2.14-inch intake valve. The engine also had an MSD ready-to-run distributor, an Edelbrock Performer RPM intake, and Comp Cams Ultra Pro Magnum rockers. With everything buttoned back up, it was time to prime the oiling system and then fire it for the first time.


Evan and Troy at Westech helped Freiburger get the 383 on the engine dyno and topped it with a 750 CFM Edelbrock VRS carb to break in the cam. After that, the inner valve springs were installed to let the engine rev up and make a full dyno run. The final numbers: 445.5 lb-ft of torque at 3500 rpm and 396.1 hp at 5400 rpm. The torque was solid, but the heads and intake have lots more horsepower potential.


If you’re not concerned with a numbers-matching build, this 383 would easily outmuscle any of the small-block V-8s available in a ’70 Duster from the factory, and several of the big-blocks that weren’t. Even as you see it in this video, off-the-shelf parts make this 383 a solid street engine. It’s not done, though. David has already swapped the hydraulic flat-tappet cam for a hydraulic roller to get a bit more power while still keeping the valves from making an abrupt introduction to the pistons. We’ll have more on that later this week.
